question: A strategy analyst is told, "Research our competitors and come back with something useful." She has two days and intends to use Claude for most of the work. What should she do first?
options: A) Ask Claude to produce a broad overview of every competitor in the sector and narrow the list afterwards.
B) Collect the competitors' public material into one place so Claude has something concrete to work from.
C) Agree with the requester which decision the research supports and which competitors and factors matter.
D) Ask Claude which competitor comparison factors are most commonly used in this kind of market study.
correct_answers: C) Agree with the requester which decision the research supports and which competitors and factors matter.
explanations: A broad sweep first spends most of the two days on competitors that will turn out to be irrelevant. Narrowing afterwards requires the very criteria the analyst has not yet agreed, so the effort has to be repeated.

Gathering source material is a sensible early move, but doing it before the question is fixed means gathering the wrong material. Which brochures, filings and reviews matter depends entirely on what the requester needs to decide.

Correct. "Something useful" is not a research question, and no amount of good prompting rescues an undefined one. Fixing the decision the work feeds and the comparison factors that bear on it determines what to gather, what to ignore, and when the analyst can stop.

Common comparison factors describe what other studies did, not what this requester needs. Adopting them substitutes a generic frame for the specific business question and leaves the analyst no closer to knowing what useful means here.
